segments.title: The Washington treaty sets the British design box
segments.body: The Washington Naval Treaty allowed Britain to build two replacement capital ships. The replacement clause also disposes of Thunderer, King George V, Ajax, and Centurion when the new ships complete, tying construction to retirement. The displacement, gun-calibre, and total-tonnage rules define the design space rather than dictating the historical Nelson layout. This makes an F2- or F3-derived alternative a change of British priorities within the same treaty settlement.

evidence.note: Britain's two replacement capital ships had to fit Washington Treaty limits of 35,000 tons and 16-inch guns, leaving a choice between the historical Nelson design and faster alternatives.

segments.summary: The treaty's 35,000-ton and 16-inch limits frame Britain's choice between a heavily protected Nelson and a faster capital ship.

segments.title: Why Tiger could outlast the older battleships
segments.body: Britain was already planning to replace the older capital ships removed under the Washington settlement. Tiger is the likely exception among the 13.5-inch-gun ships because she remained more useful than the older battleships. In the projected building sequence, the battleships disappear by the arrival of N3, with some retired when G3 enters service. Tiger could last until a following generation of fast capital ships entered service.

evidence.note: Projected G3 and N3 construction would replace the older battleships, while Tiger could survive until a later group of fast capital ships entered service.

segments.summary: Tiger's greater usefulness could keep her in service after the older 13.5-inch-gun battleships disappeared under the projected G3 and N3 building program.

segments.title: Global fleet duties favor fast capital ships
segments.body: The Royal Navy envisaged roughly 24 capital ships divided among home, Mediterranean, and eastern responsibilities. Atlantic and Indian Ocean duties required mobile ships to cover distant imperial interests, while the Mediterranean force could concentrate on battleships and reinforce the other fleets. One proposed reconstruction places all four G3s at the Eastern Fleet's core for roughly 16 to 20 years. Their dimensions suited overseas dock facilities that would be enlarged later than the home dockyards. That delay made a long useful life within the existing infrastructure especially important.

evidence.note: Home, Mediterranean, and eastern responsibilities imposed different geographic needs on Britain's planned 24-capital-ship fleet.

segments.summary: A projected 24-ship fleet needed mobile capital ships for Atlantic and Eastern Fleet coverage more than another pair optimized for a battle line.

segments.title: Nelson as the ultimate dreadnought battleship
segments.body: The Nelson design compresses N3 ideas into the treaty displacement and prioritizes armor and heavy guns. Raising B turret above A and C was intended to shorten the forward battery's footprint, although the practical space saving remains doubtful in this interpretation. The compact design was intended to operate efficiently and keep maintenance demands manageable. Its cramped arrangement nevertheless limited its suitability for long deployments to foreign stations. Hood consequently carried much of Britain's naval prestige abroad as the modern capital ship available for worldwide cruises.

evidence.note: Nelson's design priorities limited its overseas utility compared with Hood's global deployments.

segments.summary: Nelson concentrated heavy guns and armor in a treaty-sized hull, but its limitations for overseas service left Hood carrying much of Britain's naval prestige abroad.

segments.title: Postwar threat assessment rewards mobile capital ships
segments.body: The Royal Navy's late-war battlecruiser program looked beyond another North Sea battle toward peacetime presence and the next plausible opponents. The Treaty of Versailles made a rapid German return as an independent naval challenger seem unlikely, shifting attention toward Italy and Japan. Japan was still a longstanding ally, but British planners worried about its political direction. In this interpretation, Washington's treaty diplomacy gave Britain a face-saving way to end the Anglo-Japanese Alliance while publicly attributing the break to American requirements rather than a deliberate rejection of Japan.

evidence.note: Postwar British battlecruiser planning prioritized global presence as concern about Germany receded, while the Washington settlement enabled Britain to end the Anglo-Japanese Alliance.

segments.summary: Britain's post-1918 planners expected Germany to remain contained, kept building for worldwide presence, and could use the Washington settlement as a face-saving exit from an increasingly uncomfortable alliance with Japan.

segments.title: F2 and F3 as fully armored battlecruisers
segments.body: F2 offered six 15-inch guns and about 30 knots, while F3 paired nine heavy guns with slightly lower speed. In this classification, both belong to the Royal Navy's fully armored battlecruiser lineage: ships with battlecruiser-style internal subdivision but protection far beyond lightly armored speed specialists. Their ancestry runs through Tiger and G3 rather than the compromised post-Jutland development of Hood. The deciding classification feature is therefore the combination of armor coverage and subdivision throughout the hull, not belt thickness alone.

evidence.note: The F2 and F3 concepts extended the Royal Navy battlecruiser lineage represented by G3, combining speed with extensive subdivision and protection.

segments.summary: The F2 and F3 alternatives sit near the boundary between battlecruiser and fast battleship, combining high speed with serious armor.

segments.title: F2, F3, and Nelson trade speed against armor
segments.body: All three designs share a 106-foot beam, but F2 is 760 feet long overall, F3 is 740 feet, and Nelson is 710 feet. The longer F2 and F3 hulls accommodate more than twice Nelson's shaft horsepower while retaining two shafts. At deep displacement, the quoted speeds are 29.5 knots for F2, 28.5 for F3, and 23 for Nelson. F2 has a 13-inch belt over the magazines and 12 inches over machinery, while F3 has a uniform 12-inch belt. Nelson raises those figures to 14 and 13 inches respectively. The comparison places preliminary F2 and F3 designs against the modified design that became Nelson, so details such as torpedo tubes and additional anti-aircraft guns were still open to change. Forced draught offered a possible emergency speed increase at the cost of greater machinery wear.

evidence.note: F2, F3, and Nelson differed in dimensions, horsepower, speed, and armor, with additional emergency speed proposed through forced draught at increased machinery wear.

segments.summary: Dimensions, machinery, belt armor, and forced-draught speed show how much protection F3 could retain while gaining roughly six knots over Nelson.

segments.title: How could F2 and F3 make 30 knots on two shafts?
segments.body: Brown-Curtis turbines, Admiralty boilers, and a well-designed hull make about 30 knots plausible on two shafts. The shafting is also tentatively assumed to be hollow. Forced draught could raise speed beyond the quoted trial figure, with increased machinery wear. A possible wartime speed of about 26 knots for Rodney illustrates the expected emergency margin when machinery due for replacement could be driven hard enough to accept damage.

evidence.note: Modern turbines, Admiralty boilers, hull form, and possibly hollow shafting made the two-shaft speed plausible, while forced draught increased machinery wear.

segments.summary: Modern turbines, high-output boilers, and an efficient hull make the speed plausible, while forced draught buys more performance by consuming machinery life.
segments.question: How could the F2 and F3 designs reach about 30 knots with only two shafts?
segments.answerShort: By combining contemporary Brown-Curtis turbines, Admiralty boilers, and an efficient hull; forced draught could add speed, but only by increasing machinery wear.

segments.title: Is a fully armored battlecruiser halfway to a fast battleship?
segments.body: Within this classification, a fully armored battlecruiser occupies an intermediate position between a battlecruiser and a fast battleship. G3 was already moving in that direction. Its narrow British application makes another universal category less useful.

evidence.note: The intermediate position is accepted, with reluctance to add another category used so narrowly within British design practice.

segments.summary: The label works as a midpoint, but it describes a distinctly British design lineage rather than a widely populated international category.
segments.question: Could a fully armored battlecruiser be the halfway point between a battlecruiser and a fast battleship?
segments.answerShort: Yes, within this classification, although the category has such a narrow British application that adding another formal label offers limited value.

segments.title: Where would extra F3 displacement go?
segments.body: Any unused displacement could strengthen F3's belt protection. The proposed change raises the uniform 12-inch belt to 13 inches at the same inclination. That would match Nelson's machinery-belt thickness while remaining below its 14-inch magazine protection. Substantial internal and deck armor would remain part of the design.

evidence.note: Unused displacement could support a uniform 13-inch inclined belt over magazines and machinery, alongside the existing internal and deck protection.

segments.summary: Unused treaty displacement could fund a uniform 13-inch inclined belt over magazines and machinery.
segments.question: If F3 came in below the treaty limit like O3, could the unused displacement buy more armor?
segments.answerShort: Yes. The most plausible use would be a uniform 13-inch inclined belt over both magazines and machinery.

segments.title: The politics behind 'unsinkable bulwarks'
segments.body: In this interpretation, political demands for 'unsinkable bulwarks' grew from treating Jutland's battlecruiser losses primarily as a protection failure. Accepting that explanation served Beatty's interests by diverting attention from command decisions and supporting his demand for a 16-inch-gun ship. Nelson and Rodney therefore maximized armor, heavy guns, and battle-line credibility. The result was optimized for standing in a line of battle, with less speed for fast response and worldwide presence.

evidence.note: Political demands for 'unsinkable bulwarks' after Jutland, Beatty's position, and the prestige of 16-inch guns favored the heavily protected Nelson design.

segments.summary: Political memories of Jutland and prestige attached to 16-inch guns pushed Britain toward heavily protected battle-line ships.

segments.title: A thousand tons could buy Nelson more speed
segments.body: Nelson and Rodney came in roughly 1,000 to 1,500 tons below the treaty ceiling, leaving a theoretical margin for a longer hull and stronger machinery. Boiler count and steam generation, rather than turbine footprint, were the main machinery differences among the O3, F2, and F3 concepts. A bank of roughly twelve higher-output boilers instead of Nelson's eight Admiralty three-drum boilers points toward F3-like performance. Period naval architects believed two shafts could carry the power, though sustained high-speed work would increase machinery wear. Dropping to 15-inch/50 guns could free further weight, while F3's longer arrangement also improved forward gun clearance and the ability to choose the engagement angle.

evidence.note: Nelson's unused treaty margin, boiler count, two-shaft wear, 15-inch gun weight savings, and the firing-arc advantages of a longer F3-style layout all affect the redesign.

segments.summary: Nelson's margin below the 35,000-ton ceiling could fund a longer hull and more boiler power, but driving high output through two shafts would raise wear.

segments.title: Selling F3 through cost and 15-inch standardization
segments.body: The political case for F3 could emphasize Treasury savings and fleet-wide ammunition compatibility. Frederick Field's strategic ability is judged stronger here than his handling of ministers, leaving that financial case without the advocacy Henderson or Jellicoe might have supplied. The proposed 15-inch/50 used the existing 15-inch shell and breech mechanism, reducing logistical and development risk. Limited testing suggested greater range, while rearming Hood, Renown, Repulse, the Queen Elizabeths, and the Revenge class could extend their useful lives. Delaying replacement would give the Treasury a reason to support the gun beyond the cost of the two new ships.

evidence.note: Beatty's reputation and the handling of Jutland reports are offered as reasons the political case for F3 lost to heavier protection.
A proposed Treasury case combines shared ammunition, a low-risk gun development, and delayed replacement of existing ships.
The 15-inch/50 shared shells with the existing 15-inch gun family, offered greater range, and could support fleet-wide rearmament.

segments.summary: Shared ammunition and longer service lives for existing ships could make F3 attractive to the Treasury.

segments.title: Competing Jutland reports and the case for F3
segments.body: John Harper's original Jutland report and the later version overseen by Beatty support different interpretations of the battle's lessons. In the account presented here, Beatty suppressed the original because it assigned him blame and required it to be rewritten. Harper and Reginald Bacon were knowledgeable participants, but their accounts also require allowance for their own allegiances. F2, F3, G3, and N3 are linked to the earlier conclusions, while O3 and the Nelson decision reflect the later interpretation. The proposed connection between battle analysis and design therefore depends partly on how these competing accounts are read.

evidence.note: Harper's original report is contrasted with the later version overseen by Beatty and linked to competing design lessons, with an explicit warning that Harper and Bacon were not unbiased.

segments.summary: A critical account of Jutland links the original conclusions with F2, F3, G3, and N3, and the revised account with O3, while acknowledging Harper and Bacon's partisanship.

segments.title: Which books explain Royal Navy capital ships?
segments.body: John Roberts is the first recommendation for specialist studies of Royal Navy capital ships. His books include detailed plans and full deck arrangements that make design choices visible. Castles of Steel, Norman Friedman's books, and the Jutland volume shown on screen are also recommended. The wider BruShips series includes further reviews for readers pursuing a narrower battleship subject.

evidence.note: John Roberts's capital-ship studies receive the first recommendation, followed by a Jutland book whose identity depends on the visual reference.
Roberts's detailed plans, including a Warspite deck plan, support the recommendation alongside Castles of Steel, Norman Friedman's work, and further BruShips reviews.

segments.summary: John Roberts is the principal technical recommendation because his books reproduce detailed plans, with Castles of Steel and Norman Friedman's work also named.
segments.question: What are the best books on Royal Navy capital ships?
segments.answerShort: Start with John Roberts for expert studies and detailed plans; Castles of Steel and Norman Friedman's books are also useful.

segments.title: Did the 15-inch/50 use the same shell as the 15-inch/42?
segments.body: The proposed 15-inch/50 used the existing 15-inch shell. It also kept the 15-inch/42's breech mechanism. The barrel increased from 42 to 50 calibres, with limited testing suggesting greater range. A new ship would pair the weapon with the latest turret design.

evidence.note: Identical shells and breech mechanisms, the longer barrel, limited range testing, and the use of new turrets.

segments.summary: The proposed longer 15-inch gun preserved existing ammunition and breech arrangements while offering greater range.
segments.question: Did the 15-inch/50 use the same shell as the 15-inch/42?
segments.answerShort: Yes. It used the same shell and breech mechanism, with a longer barrel of 50 rather than 42 calibres.

segments.title: Presenting 15-inch guns as naval restraint
segments.body: A British choice of 15-inch guns could support a public claim of restraint while other navies adopted 16-inch weapons. In this proposed diplomatic argument, Britain would claim that experience of war had shown it did not need the larger calibre. The technical qualification is that the 15-inch/50 firing a Greenboy shell was expected to remain highly competitive in penetration. The nominal difference in calibre could therefore carry more diplomatic weight than the expected difference in fighting performance.

evidence.note: A proposed public case for 15-inch guns invokes restraint while arguing that the 15-inch/50 and Greenboy shell could match or exceed the penetration expected from a 16-inch/45.

segments.summary: Britain could present its smaller nominal calibre as restraint while retaining a weapon expected to compete with 16-inch guns.

segments.title: The counterfactual stays inside 1920 technology
segments.body: The scenario has a clear methodological limit: Britain may select another design already available in 1920, but it does not receive technology from the 1930s. The 15-inch/50 and 16-inch/45 were contemporary development choices, while a later 15-inch/45 depended on roughly another fifteen years of metallurgical work. The later gun might offer better barrel life and lower weight, but using it here would turn a decision counterfactual into a technology transplant. That boundary keeps the comparison focused on the consequences of choosing F3 rather than on an ideal ship designed with hindsight.

evidence.note: Only gun technology available in 1920 belongs in the decision; a later 1930s design is excluded.

segments.summary: Choosing the 15-inch/50 instead of the 16-inch/45 changes a historical decision without importing a later 1930s gun.

segments.title: F3 expands overseas presence and refit capacity
segments.body: F3 offered nine 15-inch/50 guns and eight 6-inch guns, with four on each side in two pairs. Space remained for 4.7-inch weapons and aircraft stowage aft. Its draught and hull form supported worldwide operations, while its speed made distant deployments and returns more practical. With six fast capital ships, overseas cruises would no longer place such a heavy burden on Hood. Two ships could enter refit while four remained available, strengthening the case for keeping Tiger in service or using her for gunnery training.

evidence.note: F3's armament, aircraft space, draught, and speed support overseas service, while six fast capital ships allow two to undergo refit with four still available.

segments.summary: Fast Nelson replacements join Hood, Tiger, Renown, and Repulse in a larger deployable pool for cruises, deterrence, and refits.

segments.title: German test pieces did not guarantee production quality
segments.body: The explanation for Britain's 16-inch gun problems centers on a misleading inference from tests of German guns. A false positive encouraged a design philosophy that later testing undermined. British gun and armor metallurgy is judged superior in this assessment, so inferior British materials are rejected as the cause. British and American examinations after World War II are cited for serious German battleship-armor quality-control problems. The production problem was maintaining the quality of experimental work across the volume of armor required.

evidence.note: A false positive in German-gun testing is distinguished from metallurgy, followed by a critical assessment of German armor quality control based on British and American postwar examinations.

segments.summary: British gun philosophy could take a false lesson from German test results even though later Allied inspection judged British metallurgy and German armor consistency very differently.

segments.title: Why is King George V's belt quoted as both 14.7 and 15 inches?
segments.body: The King George V-class belt figure given here is 14.7 inches, with some sources rounding it to 15. Royal Navy armor orders specified weight over a defined area. Historians convert such specifications into familiar inch measurements to compare navies that ordered armor differently. Those figures are standardized equivalents and should not be mistaken for the language of the original order.

evidence.note: The 14.7-inch figure is sometimes rounded to 15 inches, while British armor orders specified weight over an area.

segments.summary: The 15-inch figure rounds a 14.7-inch equivalent, while the original British procurement specification expressed armor by weight over an area.
segments.question: Was the King George V-class belt 14.7 inches or 15 inches thick?
segments.answerShort: The comparison uses 14.7 inches; some accounts round it to 15. British armor orders specified weight over an area, which historians convert into thickness for comparison.

segments.title: An F3 cruise turns Tsushima's anniversary into naval diplomacy
segments.body: The Special Service Squadron's earlier Empire Cruise provides the model for a later F3 deployment. In the proposed 1929-30 cruise, Nelson and Rodney could visit Japan for Tsushima's twenty-fifth anniversary and show Britain's newest capital ships to Admiral Togo Heihachiro. The visit would emphasize the old Anglo-Japanese friendship during a period of renewed treaty bargaining. This is a suggested diplomatic use for the hypothetical ships, whose speed and endurance would let them make regular overseas appearances.

evidence.note: A proposed 1929-30 F3 world cruise reaches Japan for Tsushima's twenty-fifth anniversary, supporting friendship and treaty diplomacy.

segments.summary: A proposed 1929-30 cruise could take the fast Nelson and Rodney to Japan to mark Tsushima's twenty-fifth anniversary and display British naval capability.

segments.title: A fast flying squadron built around carriers
segments.body: Tiger and the two F3-derived ships would form a division near 28 knots, while Hood, Renown, and Repulse formed another near 32 knots. Adding three fast carriers and cruisers would support detachments built around one or two carriers and two to four capital ships. By about 1930, the proposed force could acquire a vice-admiral's command with separate senior officers responsible for the capital-ship divisions and carriers. Distant deployments by this force would leave the Queen Elizabeth and Revenge classes available for local duties and better maintenance. Courageous or Glorious could also accompany the hypothetical Nelson and Rodney on a world cruise, making carrier operations part of the same overseas presence.

evidence.note: Two divisions of fast capital ships and three carriers support balanced deployments, a proposed senior command structure, and relief for older battleships' overseas duties.

segments.summary: Two fast capital-ship divisions and three carriers could evolve into a global response force years before wartime carrier task groups.

segments.title: Fast capital ships could reshape British cruisers
segments.body: The alternate capital-ship decision could influence the cruisers expected to accompany the flying squadron. An F3-like forward armament arrangement is suggested for the projected Surrey class, while building the fuller design could avoid what the criticism of the smaller Yorks identifies as inadequate savings for their lost capability. If all five Surreys entered service before the London treaty, Britain would approach it with a much larger force of County-family heavy cruisers. The rough total reaches eighteen such ships, making the capital-ship choice a broader influence on cruiser procurement and fleet appearance.

evidence.note: An F3-style Surrey is proposed in place of the York economies, with five hypothetical ships increasing the County-family total to roughly eighteen.
The proposed Surrey layout places its 8-inch guns forward and heavy anti-aircraft armament aft.

segments.summary: An F3-style fleet aesthetic and operating concept might favor fuller Surrey-class construction over compromised York-class economies.

segments.title: American and Japanese navies confront a faster battle line
segments.body: In the scenario, attention to gun calibre could obscure the operational problem posed by six British capital ships able to make at least 28 knots. A 21-knot American battle line would struggle to dictate range against them. The cancelled Lexington battlecruisers leave a gap that their carrier conversions do not fill as fast gunnery ships. Japan's four Kongos would face six British fast ships, while adding the Nagatos would lower the Japanese force's speed. Comparing published figures also requires care because British speeds excluded forced draught while Japanese figures tended to include it.

evidence.note: Six roughly 28-knot British capital ships would outpace US standard battleships and outnumber the four Kongos, while adding Nagato would slow the Japanese force.

segments.summary: A six-ship British fast force would challenge the slower US battle line and force Japan to choose between Kongo's speed and reinforcement by the slower Nagatos.

segments.title: Carriers were coming, not yet dominant, in 1930
segments.body: The counterfactual does not assume that everyone in 1930 could reason from wartime carrier experience. Aircraft carriers were an emerging capability, but the aircraft available in 1930 had not yet given them the capabilities demonstrated during World War II. Naval planners therefore still had to compare battle-line speed, range control, and gun power. That period perspective explains why a faster British battle line could remain a concern even as carriers developed.

evidence.note: Carriers remained an emerging rather than mature weapon in 1930, so battle-line speed still dominated contemporary planning.

segments.summary: Early carriers mattered, but contemporary aircraft performance left battle-line speed and gunnery central to American and Japanese reactions.

segments.title: France and Italy face new capital-ship choices
segments.body: The Dunkerques would still strengthen an allied fast force, although Britain would depend less heavily on their contribution if Nelson and Rodney already had F3 speed. The older French and Italian battleships would face a harder comparison with that British force. Rebuilt Italian ships reaching about 26 knots would remain slow enough for F3 to catch, making new construction more attractive than further expensive alterations. The scenario expects French finances to constrain a response, while Mussolini's prestige ambitions make a new Italian 28-knot design more plausible. These are proposed reactions to the altered British fleet.

evidence.note: Dunkerque remains useful but less essential to Britain's fast force, while French financial constraints and Italian prestige ambitions shape different possible responses.

segments.summary: Dunkerque remains useful to Britain, while the altered speed balance could make new Italian ships more attractive than rebuilding older hulls.

segments.title: A London treaty bargain permits new battleships
segments.body: The proposed bargain allows five new ships each for Britain and the United States, three for Japan, and two each for France and Italy. A speed cap cannot solve the imbalance without forcing Britain to surrender Hood, Renown, and Repulse or allowing replacement ships that deepen British modernization. The controlled option spreads construction across roughly six years and lets each signatory replace older hulls without abandoning the ratio system. The plausible outcomes are treaty collapse, the historical settlement despite continuing resentment, or that limited new-building agreement.

evidence.note: The proposed London settlement assigns construction quotas, rejects a speed limit as unworkable, and leaves several possible treaty outcomes.

segments.summary: Dissatisfaction with British fleet speed could replace the battleship holiday with a limited six-year construction program.

segments.title: Japan could replace Fuso and Ise while retaining Kongo
segments.body: Japan's proposed three-ship allowance raises the question of which existing battleships to replace. The likely candidates are the two Fusos and one Ise-class ship, whose roughly 23-knot speed leaves them behind the new fast ships. The Kongos offer more scope for further development and would therefore be stronger candidates for retention. This is a proposed replacement sequence within the counterfactual treaty settlement.

evidence.note: The proposed Japanese replacement sequence favors the slower Fuso and Ise classes over the more adaptable Kongos.

segments.summary: Three permitted replacements would favor retiring slower Fuso- and Ise-class ships while preserving the Kongos' greater development potential.

segments.title: Could Depression shipyards absorb five new battleships?
segments.body: The proposed five-battleship program spreads its orders across six years. Shipyards looking for work would have room for the additional construction, while depressed wages would reduce its cost. On that basis, the program could fit alongside other orders during the Depression.

evidence.note: A five-ship, six-year program need not displace other orders and could exploit low wages and shipyards seeking work during the Depression.

segments.summary: A measured five-battleship program over six years could exploit low costs and idle capacity rather than crowd out the rest of the fleet.
segments.question: Could the United States order five battleships during the Depression without disrupting other construction?
segments.answerShort: In the proposed six-year program, yes: shipyards were seeking work and depressed wages reduced costs, allowing the orders to fit alongside other construction.

segments.title: Why a construction holiday disadvantaged Japan
segments.body: A building holiday affected navies with different industrial capacities unevenly. Britain and the United States could expand construction more readily when restrictions ended, whereas Japan depended more heavily on keeping its own construction moving. Permission to build several ships would therefore address part of Japan's dissatisfaction with the treaty system. The proposed compromise still leaves room for understated displacement figures, including a hypothetical 40,000-ton ship declared as 35,000 tons.

evidence.note: Japan's limited ability to expand construction quickly provides a reason to accept renewed building within the treaty system, with possible understatement of displacement.

segments.summary: Japan's weaker ability to expand production quickly gave it an industrial reason to prefer limited, continuing battleship construction.

segments.title: Keeping 15-inch guns saves weight throughout the ship
segments.body: Britain could retain the 15-inch/50 in another generation of fast capital ships if the F3-derived arrangement had proved satisfactory. Moving to 16-inch guns remained an option, but the smaller calibre offered cumulative weight savings. The ammunition allowance, gun barrels, and ammunition-handling equipment would each be lighter. Together, those savings make continued use of 15-inch guns a plausible British choice while the American and Japanese designs move toward 16-inch armament.

evidence.note: The proposed 15-inch/50 saves weight across ammunition, barrels, and handling systems, supporting its continued use in British fast capital ships.

segments.summary: Retaining the proposed 15-inch/50 armament saves weight in the ammunition, barrels, and handling equipment of a treaty-limited battleship.

segments.title: Naval treaties tolerated a bounded margin of misstatement
segments.body: Naval architects in each power could compare declared dimensions, armor, machinery, and armament and recognize when the published displacement did not add up. Exact proof was harder, and every major navy exploited definitions or understated figures to some degree. The treaties worked by keeping these departures within a tolerable range rather than enforcing perfect honesty. British designers were especially adept at using the written definitions, such as excluding water carried for armor protection from standard displacement, while other navies more visibly broke the letter of the rules.

evidence.note: By comparing declared dimensions, armor, machinery, and armament, naval architects could spot suspect displacement figures. Treaty practice tolerated limited departures, while British standard-displacement definitions advantaged British designs.

segments.summary: Design bureaus could detect implausible specifications, but the treaty system aimed to contain cheating within a known band rather than secure literal precision.

segments.title: An early King George V program replaces the R class
segments.body: Under the proposed London treaty quota, Britain can build five capital ships between 1931 and 1936, so the next name in the sequence becomes an earlier King George V class. The likely design retains the F3-derived emphasis on about 28 knots and nine 15-inch guns rather than returning to a slow battle-line ship. These ships would most plausibly replace the Revenge or R class, while Tiger could survive as a gunnery-training and relief ship within the faster fleet. The five new ships and the F3-derived Nelson and Rodney would provide seven ships capable of roughly 28 knots. Alongside the three faster battlecruisers, they would leave the five Queen Elizabeths as the slower part of the proposed fifteen-ship fleet.

evidence.note: An early five-ship King George V program would likely combine nine 15-inch guns with a speed of about 28 knots and replace the R class.

segments.summary: Five early-1930s, 28-knot ships carrying nine 15-inch guns would replace the R class and extend F3 priorities into a new King George V class.

segments.title: Queen Elizabeth rebuilds complete a 28-knot battle line
segments.body: A new five-ship program would keep yards and suppliers active while the Royal Navy modernized its surviving First World War capital ships. The proposal runs the R class hard as near-term cover while rebuilding the Queen Elizabeths with new boilers, turbines, and shafts. Reaching 28 knots might require forced draught, but their four-shaft arrangement makes a major increase more plausible. Combined with Hood, Renown, Repulse, the F3 pair, and five new ships, the reconstructions would turn British battle-line speed from a specialist advantage into a fleet-wide operating standard.

evidence.note: A new construction program would lower the cost of Queen Elizabeth-class reconstructions, with the R class covering the rebuilding period and 28 knots as the battle line's target speed.

segments.summary: Concurrent new construction could make deep Queen Elizabeth-class machinery rebuilds cheaper and leave Britain with an almost uniformly fast capital fleet.

segments.title: An earlier US fast-battleship program could change fleet operations
segments.body: The proposed American quota replaces older battleships with five fast ships armed with the 16-inch/45. The gun choice distinguishes contemporary weapons from the later 16-inch/50 design, rather than denying the existence of earlier guns of that calibre and length. The new ships could operate with Lexington and Saratoga and give the US Navy experience coordinating fast capital ships and carriers in the early 1930s. Sustaining that force could also encourage orders for faster fleet oilers, because auxiliaries otherwise limit operational pace. British base chains shorten their oilers' shuttle routes, whereas American tankers must support movement across the Pacific. These are possible operational developments before the historical North Carolinas entered service.

evidence.note: Replacing older US battleships with five 28-knot ships armed with 16-inch/45 guns could provide earlier fast-carrier experience and a reason to order faster oilers.

segments.summary: Five early 28-knot battleships could give the US Navy more experience combining fast capital ships with carriers.

segments.title: Were 16-inch/50 guns already available for the cancelled American ships?
segments.body: The choice of 16-inch/45 guns for the proposed early-1930s battleships depends on which 16-inch/50 design is meant. Successive gun designs can share a nominal calibre and barrel length. Later metallurgy and development separate the later 16-inch/50 from the weapons intended for the cancelled Lexington and South Dakota designs. The hypothetical early construction program therefore retains the 16-inch/45.

evidence.note: The earlier Lexington and South Dakota guns are distinguished from the later 16-inch/50 through metallurgy and development.

segments.summary: The earlier Lexington and South Dakota weapons must be distinguished from the later 16-inch/50 used in the design comparison.
segments.question: Didn't the Lexington and South Dakota designs already have 16-inch/50 guns?
segments.answerShort: Those earlier guns were a different design from the later 16-inch/50 under discussion, which depended on subsequent metallurgy and gun development.

segments.title: Does a ship's reputation pass to its namesake?
segments.body: Warspite is offered as a relatively consistent example of an inherited reputation, while Dreadnought and Prince of Wales illustrate how differently successive namesakes can fare. Some Prince of Wales ships are remembered as successful, while others suffered conspicuously bad luck. A pair of namesakes provides little material for this sort of comparison; a name reused seven, eight, or more times offers a longer historical record. Frequent name reuse makes the Royal Navy a useful source of examples.

evidence.note: Warspite and Dreadnought illustrate contrasting reputations across reused Royal Navy names.
Prince of Wales supplies another example of differing fortunes, and a long sequence of namesakes offers more historical material than only two ships.

segments.summary: Repeated names invite comparisons across generations, but the fortunes of Dreadnought and Prince of Wales do not follow a consistent pattern.
segments.question: Does a ship's reputation or 'machine spirit' always transfer with its name?
segments.answerShort: Successive namesakes can have very different records. Warspite, Dreadnought, and Prince of Wales provide contrasting examples of the apparent continuity and changes in a ship name's fortunes.

segments.title: New treaty quotas accelerate Italian and French design choices
segments.body: Limited new-building quotas would give each power a different answer. Italy's historical Littorio and Vittorio Veneto were laid down in 1934, making a broadly Littorio-style, nine-15-inch-gun response plausible within this accelerated timeline, though exact technology still constrains the design. France had smaller-gun and tonnage options rather than simply copying Britain. One calculation combines 70,000 tons for two new ships with 53,000 tons already available, allowing four roughly 30,000-ton ships capable of about 28 to 29 knots and carrying twelve 13-inch guns in three quadruple turrets. Treaty ratios and industrial starting points therefore produce different fast-battleship solutions.

evidence.note: Possible foreign responses include an early Littorio-like Italian ship and French 30,000-ton designs with twelve 13-inch guns in quadruple turrets.

segments.summary: Italy could pursue a Littorio-like 15-inch ship earlier, while France might turn its available tonnage into several 28-knot ships with quadruple 13-inch turrets.

segments.title: New construction ripples into carriers and Soviet battleships
segments.body: Capital-ship building would likely be accompanied by additional carrier orders as navies assemble balanced fast forces. British experience with a flying squadron could also justify more than the historical Ark Royal order and sharpen carrier-number bargaining at the next treaty. Outside the treaty system, Soviet leaders could face pressure to order Project 21 around 1933, potentially putting ships into service by 1939. Meanwhile, a Royal Navy with many 28-knot capital ships can hunt Deutschland-class commerce raiders, weakening the operational premise behind further ships of that type.

evidence.note: Possible consequences include additional carriers, earlier Soviet Project 21 construction, and greater vulnerability of Deutschland-class raiders to fast British capital ships.

segments.summary: Resumed battleship construction could encourage more carriers, bring Soviet Project 21 forward, and weaken the Deutschland class's advantage in speed.

segments.title: Ship names shape crew culture
segments.body: In this explanation, 'machine spirit' refers to the expectations and culture that build around a ship's name. Certain names attract inherited expectations, and crews then act within that culture. Tribal-class destroyer sailors saw themselves as the elite of an already elite branch, reinforced by names chosen for martial associations and by a role leading other destroyers. Assignments to names such as Warspite, Dreadnought, Ark Royal, or Enterprise could similarly make sailors feel accountable to earlier ships. Alex Clarke recalls visiting HMS Illustrious in service and finding that her crew took their history seriously, with particular importance attached to Taranto Night.

evidence.note: Tribal-class elite identity and famous inherited names illustrate crew expectations, while Alex Clarke's visit to HMS Illustrious supplies personal testimony about Taranto Night.

segments.summary: Inherited names and martial associations can shape the expectations crews have of themselves and their role.

segments.title: The arms race reshapes late-1930s fleets
segments.body: Britain enters later construction with active armor production and recent design experience, avoiding some historical King George V delays. Soviet building could encourage Japanese demands for a larger fleet allowance, increasing the British and American totals under the existing ratio. A follow-on treaty could repeat the new-building quotas, but any increase in Japan's allowance would force the British and American totals upward as well. Hitler is still likely to seek battleships for prestige, but he confronts a Royal Navy already approaching twenty capital ships. Beyond this point, the timing and shape of a European war become too contingent for firm prediction.

evidence.note: The construction cascade reaches Britain, Germany, the Soviet Union, and Japan, after which the scenario becomes too contingent for reliable extrapolation.

segments.summary: Earlier British, American, and Soviet construction drives further German and Japanese demands and makes the road to World War II highly uncertain.

segments.title: Fleet confidence changes diplomacy and frustrates a submarine offset
segments.body: Conventional deterrence is partly psychological: a government negotiates differently when a modern fleet already exists behind its claims. Seven recent fast capital ships, reconstructed older ships, and a continuing destroyer program would make Britain less anxious during the later 1930s. Germany might answer this material advantage with a submarine-focused offset strategy, but concentrating on one threat also makes German intentions easier to counter. Treaty rules limited a sloop's size, armament, and designed speed but not the number built, allowing Britain and the dominions to mass-produce anti-submarine escorts and weapons before war. Hermann Göring's hostility to naval spending would also constrain Germany's shipbuilding within the rearmament program. That constraint helps explain the historically small U-boat force at the outbreak of war.

evidence.note: A stronger fleet would bolster British political confidence, while a predictable German submarine strategy could prompt early mass construction of treaty-exempt escorts; Hermann Göring's funding priorities would further constrain German naval expansion.

segments.summary: Earlier British rearmament strengthens political confidence, while a German turn to submarines invites a predictable mass response in treaty-exempt escorts.

segments.title: Could Australian docks support a Queen Elizabeth?
segments.body: Australia possessed more suitable dry-dock capacity in the late 1930s than survived by the 2024 recording. At least a couple of facilities could accommodate a Queen Elizabeth-class battleship. Much of that capacity was later lost when docks were filled in during the 1970s. Operating battleships during World War II might have encouraged Australia to preserve more of those facilities.

evidence.note: A couple of Australian docks could accommodate a Queen Elizabeth-class battleship before later dock infilling, including during the 1970s.

segments.summary: Late-1930s Australia had at least a couple of docks able to support major warships, with more heavy infrastructure than survived later postwar rationalization.
segments.question: How many Australian dry docks could take a Queen Elizabeth-class ship by the late 1930s?
segments.answerShort: At least a couple could, because Australia then retained more major dry-dock capacity than survived the dock closures and infilling of the 1970s.

segments.title: Were Britain and the United States already naval partners?
segments.body: American political avoidance of European alliances did not prevent naval planning in Asia, where both services expected they would probably fight Japan together. Cooperation built from their wartime experience and was underway by about 1924, helping later joint systems appear quickly during the Second World War. Economic competition and political rhetoric continued between the two countries. Neither navy treated active war between Britain and the United States as the likely strategic problem.

evidence.note: Formal American non-alliance is distinguished from mid-1920s naval cooperation against a possible Japanese threat.

segments.summary: Formal American non-alliance in Europe coexisted with naval cooperation from the mid-1920s against a possible war with Japan.
segments.question: Was the United States too non-aligned in the 1920s for close naval cooperation with Britain?
segments.answerShort: No. Washington avoided European alliances, but the British and American navies cooperated from about 1924 because both expected partnership in a possible Asian war with Japan.

segments.title: Why did the League of Nations lack teeth?
segments.body: The interwar organization was the League of Nations, not the later United Nations. Although Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points shaped the League, the US Congress kept the United States out. The institution therefore depended heavily on Britain and France to turn decisions into action. If treaty constraints and weak defenses left those states unwilling to enforce a ruling, the League became a forum without coercive power. The later UN Security Council offers a comparison for similar veto and enforcement limits.

evidence.note: The League's organization is clarified: the United States did not join, and enforcement depended on British and French willingness and capacity.

segments.summary: The League could act only when major members were willing and able to enforce its decisions, while the United States never joined.
segments.question: Was the United Nations the organization shaping interwar enforcement?
segments.answerShort: No. It was the League of Nations, and it lacked force when the United States stayed out and Britain and France would not or could not enforce its decisions.

segments.title: How tall was Nelson's armor belt?
segments.body: Nelson's armor belt provided heavy, full-dreadnought coverage. Its numerical height is not given in this brief answer.

evidence.note: Heavy, full-dreadnought belt coverage, without a numerical height.

segments.summary: Nelson's belt had heavy, full-dreadnought coverage, although no numerical height is supplied.
segments.question: How tall was Nelson's armor belt?
segments.answerShort: It had heavy, full-dreadnought coverage, although no numeric belt height is given in this exchange.

segments.title: Could a fast carrier squadron accelerate naval aviation?
segments.body: Including carriers in the flying squadron and its global cruise could raise their public and institutional profile. Appointing a Rear Admiral Aircraft Carriers in 1928 would bring the post forward by about two years and might accelerate the settlement over control of naval aviation. Earlier naval control would let procurement battles concentrate on acquiring aircraft for the Fleet Air Arm. Ideas for overseas aircraft factories had appeared in position papers from individual officers, and an earlier settlement might give those proposals more time to develop. Supermarine, Fairey, and Blackburn factories in Ceylon could supply aircraft to the Royal Navy and potentially to British, Australian, and New Zealand air forces in the region. Engine production would remain the major question: a Rolls-Royce or Bristol shadow factory would determine which engines the regional factories could obtain.

evidence.note: Earlier carrier command and Fleet Air Arm control could strengthen individual officers' proposals for Ceylon aircraft factories, with engine production a major constraint.

segments.summary: Earlier carrier command could shift interservice politics toward acquiring aircraft and support an imperial production network around Ceylon.
segments.question: Would carriers in a 28-knot flying squadron gain a larger public role and bring the Fleet Air Arm under naval control sooner?
segments.answerShort: It could raise the carriers' profile and bring naval control of the Fleet Air Arm forward, allowing earlier attention to aircraft procurement and proposals for overseas factories.

segments.title: Could the Deutschland class be made faster?
segments.body: Contemporary diesels allowed only a limited increase in Deutschland's speed. A larger increase would require a steam plant and a changed ship design. Combining steam machinery with an all-forward armament would also require a different layout. Such a ship is considered possible, but it would differ substantially from the historical Deutschland class.

evidence.note: Diesel machinery could provide Deutschland only a limited speed gain; a larger increase would require steam machinery and a different internal and armament layout.

segments.summary: Diesels allow only a modest gain; a major speed increase requires steam machinery and therefore a substantially different internal and armament layout.
segments.question: Could the Deutschland-class ships be made significantly faster?
segments.answerShort: Not on the same diesel arrangement. A major speed gain would require steam machinery and a substantially redesigned ship.

segments.title: Japan's 10:7 demand changes the treaty fleet balance
segments.body: A hypothetical ceiling of 25 capital ships each for Britain and the United States gives Japan 15 under a 5:3 ratio. The desired 10:7 relationship instead produces an allowance equivalent to 17.5 ships. Rounding that allowance to 18 is proposed as the likely practical settlement. Each 25-ship fleet would still retain a seven-ship numerical advantage over Japan.

evidence.note: The hypothetical calculation compares 15 Japanese ships under 5:3 with about 18 under 10:7, against British and American fleets of 25.

segments.summary: At a 25-ship British and American ceiling, Japan receives 15 ships under 5:3 but about 18 under the desired 10:7 ratio.

segments.title: Ceylon factories could shorten North African supply routes
segments.body: A Rolls-Royce factory in Ceylon could encourage the army to establish tank production nearby. With suitable factories and tooling, the region's raw materials could support a wider wartime supply hub. Starting that development in 1937 is proposed as a way to make the infrastructure available for the war. Some supplies for North Africa could then come from Ceylon instead of traveling from Britain around Africa. The benefit depends on establishing production capacity before those supplies are needed.

evidence.note: Conditional aircraft-engine and tank production in Ceylon, beginning with factories and tooling, could shorten supply routes to North Africa.

segments.summary: Engine production in Ceylon could support a wider industrial hub and shorten supply routes to the North African campaign.

segments.title: Does the Royal Navy need an ultra-long-range cruiser?
segments.body: The mission did not reward maximizing range at the expense of every other quality. British cruisers had to return for ammunition resupply and gun-barrel replacement even if their fuel endurance increased. Peacetime deployments also moved from port to port to display presence, while wartime operations used a dense imperial base network. Spending displacement on extreme range could therefore sacrifice speed or armor without creating a capability the Royal Navy actually lacked.

evidence.note: The need for extreme cruiser range is challenged against armor, speed, resupply, and base-supported presence missions.

segments.summary: Britain's base chain and port-to-port presence missions make extreme endurance less valuable than speed or protection bought with the same displacement.
segments.question: Why would the Royal Navy need an ultra-long-range cruiser?
segments.answerShort: It generally would not: overseas bases and port visits already supported its missions, so the same displacement was more useful in speed or armor.

segments.title: How was Britain meant to defend Singapore?
segments.body: Britain's defense plan used T-class submarines to ambush Japanese fleets and forces approaching Singapore. Mediterranean demands drew away submarines, while troops trained for the region went to North Africa and replacements had less familiarity with the terrain. Local priorities favored Malaya's economic role, and the assessment here is sharply critical of the army leadership assigned to its defense. Reinforcements and supplies were expected to travel through the Mediterranean and Suez Canal, or around Africa if necessary, before reaching Singapore through the Indian Ocean. The plan then envisaged operations up the South China Sea. France's defeat and Japanese access to Indochina, together with the collapse of the Philippines, disrupted assumptions about the time available. Whether those plans were adequate is a separate question from what British planners actually intended.

evidence.note: Submarine and troop diversions, criticism of Malayan preparation, British supply routes, and the collapse of assumptions about French and Philippine resistance.

segments.summary: The planned defense combined submarines, regional forces, and trained ground troops, but Mediterranean and North African demands stripped away key assets.
segments.question: How could Britain defend Singapore before the United States entered the war?
segments.answerShort: Use submarines and prepared regional forces, but the historical plan was hollowed out by diversions to the Mediterranean and North Africa, weak local command, and Japanese access through French Indochina.

segments.title: The Indian Ocean brought three Axis submarine services together
segments.body: The wartime division described here gave the United States the lead in the Pacific and Britain the lead in the Indian Ocean, alongside its Atlantic and Mediterranean commitments. Japanese, German, and Italian submarines all operated in the Indian Ocean, at times from bases on the Malayan Peninsula. Their activity provides a qualified opportunity to compare the operational methods of the three services within one theater.

evidence.note: British Indian Ocean responsibility and the qualified opportunity to compare Japanese, German, and Italian submarine operations there.

segments.summary: British responsibility in the Indian Ocean put the Royal Navy against Japanese, German, and Italian submarines operating from the Malayan region.

segments.title: British and American Pacific range needs differ
segments.body: Town- and County-class cruisers had sufficient range for Britain's existing Far Eastern deployments and overseas bases. Peacetime deterrence required regular visits to foreign ports as well as ships available at sea. British operations were expected to run through the South China Sea, East China Sea, and Sea of Japan. American forces faced a trans-Pacific approach, creating different endurance requirements. Fuel endurance has to be judged against those routes and the port visits required for presence missions.

evidence.note: Britain's overseas base network supported operations through Asian seas, whereas American planners needed trans-Pacific endurance.

segments.summary: British ships operated along an overseas base chain and up Asian seas, while American forces needed the endurance to cross the Pacific.

segments.title: Canadian funding limited prewar armament
segments.body: Britain supplied Canada with as much armament as the Canadian government was willing to finance.

evidence.note: Canadian willingness to pay is identified as the constraint on British provision of armaments.

segments.summary: Canada received armament up to the level its government was willing to finance.

segments.title: American resources and Britain's convoy problem
segments.body: American resources were available for Britain to use in both world wars. In this assessment, they mattered more to Britain in World War I because British reluctance to adopt convoys increased its difficulties. American entry came late in both wars, so material support and formal participation need to be considered separately.

evidence.note: The comparison links Britain's need for American resources in World War I to reluctance over convoys and notes late American entry into both wars.

segments.summary: British reluctance to adopt convoys is offered as a reason American resources mattered particularly in World War I.

segments.title: What did American neutrality mean before World War I entry?
segments.body: Legal belligerence and economic participation were different questions. Before entering the First World War, the United States supplied weapons and other material rather than remaining commercially detached. Once America joined, shortages also led it to buy equipment from Britain and France. 'Neutral' is therefore an incomplete description of wartime logistics and alliance dependence.

evidence.note: The United States remained formally neutral while supplying arms, then bought equipment from Britain and France after entering the war.

segments.summary: Formal neutrality did not prevent American arms trading, and after US entry the material relationship also ran in the other direction.
segments.question: How neutral was the United States before entering the First World War?
segments.answerShort: Neutral in formal belligerent status, but not economically detached: American firms supplied arms, and after entry the United States also bought equipment from Britain and France.

segments.title: Imperial infrastructure and the limits of historical expertise
segments.body: The British Empire supplied an extensive pool of infrastructure, but its administration and historical interpretation raise wider questions. Alex Clarke argues that Cold War perspectives influenced later views of empires and recalls conversations with historians from other countries, including the Congo. His comparative judgment is that Britain could have used and administered imperial resources better, while some other imperial systems were worse. He presents that as a qualified assessment and explicitly declines to claim expertise in colonial administration, distinguishing it from his work on naval history, economics, and politics.

evidence.note: Alex Clarke's comparative judgment about empires draws on personal conversations with historians and his view of Cold War influences on interpretation.
An explicit limit on expertise in colonial administration distinguishes it from naval history, economics, and politics.

segments.summary: A discussion of imperial infrastructure turns to Cold War influences on historical interpretation, personal conversations, and the limits of expertise in colonial administration.

segments.title: Earlier Alaska-type cruisers would depend on the treaties
segments.body: The altered construction sequence could bring large cruisers such as the Alaska class forward. Whether that happens remains dependent on the treaty framework, so earlier construction is a possible consequence rather than a settled part of the scenario.

evidence.note: Earlier Alaska-class construction is suggested conditionally, with the treaty situation left as the deciding constraint.

segments.summary: Earlier large cruisers are a possible consequence of the altered building programs, subject to continuing treaty restrictions.

segments.title: What makes an ideal warship design?
segments.body: An ideal ship depends on its period and the resources available to build it. Malta and Midway are the personal carrier preferences for the World War II period. In the game Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts, the usual battleship preference is nine to twelve 16.5-inch guns and at least 28 knots. Those figures describe a game design choice. The Daring class is the favored destroyer example.

evidence.note: Personal carrier and destroyer preferences, plus explicitly game-based battleship choices in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.

segments.summary: Personal design preferences include Malta and Midway carriers, Daring-class destroyers, and heavily armed battleships built in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts.
segments.question: What is your ideal ship?
segments.answerShort: The preference depends on the period: Malta or Midway among World War II carriers, the Daring class among destroyers, and game-designed battleships with nine to twelve 16.5-inch guns and at least 28 knots.

segments.title: Should Britain have adopted more diesel propulsion?
segments.body: Germany's existing industrial infrastructure supported diesel machinery. Britain would have needed to fund the construction capacity, support systems, and training required for a larger shift to diesel, taking resources from other naval priorities. Continuing with steam is therefore the preference here. The British wartime plant is associated with a design choice around 1935, compared with American choices around 1937-38. Selecting a later British boiler design could have brought higher pressure, improved efficiency, and greater range.

evidence.note: Existing diesel infrastructure in Germany, the cost of creating a British equivalent, and the proposed range benefit of choosing a later steam-boiler design.

segments.summary: Britain's existing steam infrastructure made turbines the economical choice, though a later boiler design freeze could have improved efficiency.
segments.question: Should Britain have used more diesel power plants before World War II?
segments.answerShort: Probably not: Britain's industrial and training base favored steam, though adopting a later, higher-pressure boiler standard could have delivered better efficiency.

segments.title: What would a 4,000-BM-ton warship look like in a 1799 scenario?
segments.body: For this role-playing scenario, the proposed ship is a very large, fast frigate with one principal gun deck. Its gun total might approach a fourth rate, while the single-deck arrangement leads to a fifth- or sixth-rate classification in the answer. It would be a new design, rather than a razee cut down from a larger ship. Armament would depend on the intended navy: a British version would favor long guns for their range when pursuing and engaging privateers, while carronades are suggested as a possibility for an American version. The later follow-up specifies tons BM, although its tentative comparison with a named ship is unclear in the captions.

evidence.note: A role-playing scenario produces a fast, single-gun-deck frigate, with rating, razee, and long-gun versus carronade distinctions.
The follow-up specifies 4,000 BM tons; the comparison offered from memory contains an unclear ship name.

segments.summary: A 1799 role-playing scenario produces a large, fast single-gun-deck frigate, with British armament favoring long guns for range.
segments.question: In a role-playing game set in 1799, what would a privately designed 4,000-BM-ton warship be like?
segments.answerShort: A very large, fast single-deck frigate, classified here as a fifth or sixth rate and, in British service, favoring long guns for range against privateers.
